ads.headline: Take back control of your blood sugar naturally
ads.primaryText:
I changed my diet. I walked every day. I cut sugar completely. My A1C was still 6.1.

Then I found something. Four months later, A1C 5.6. No Metformin.

I'm a pharmacist. 28 years. Here's what I found.

I've filled thousands of Metformin prescriptions. Thousands. Watched the bottles go out the door every single day. "First line treatment for Type 2 diabetes," the guidelines say.

I've also watched what happens to the people who come back.

The stomach problems that never fully go away. Nausea every morning. Diarrhea that comes without warning. I've had patients whisper to me at the counter, embarrassed, asking if it ever gets better. Most of the time, I have to tell them their body "should adjust." Knowing full well that for many, it never does.

The fatigue. Patients who were sharp, active, present — now dragging themselves through the door looking ten years older. Picking up their refill and a coffee, trying to get through another day.

The neuropathy that creeps in anyway. Even with "controlled" A1C. Tingling that becomes numbness. Numbness that becomes falls. Falls that become fractures. And I'm the one handing them yet another prescription — now for nerve pain on top of the diabetes medication.

The vitamin B12 depletion that nobody warns them about. Metformin blocks B12 absorption. So now they're tired, foggy, and their doctor adds another pill. Then another. I've watched patients go from one medication to four in three years. Then six. Then a plastic organizer, Sunday through Saturday.

So when my own blood work came back — A1C 6.3, fasting glucose 118 — and my doctor said "prediabetic, six months to bring it down or we start Metformin," I smiled politely and said I'd work on lifestyle changes.

But I already knew I wasn't going to take it.

I'd seen too much from the other side of the counter. I wasn't going down that road.

So I researched alternatives. Everything pointed to Ceylon cinnamon.

Polyphenols that mimic insulin. Improved cellular glucose uptake. Slowed carbohydrate breakdown. Studies from the USDA showing cinnamon compounds increased glucose metabolism 20-fold. A 2019 UCLA clinical trial — specifically on prediabetics — showing significant improvements in fasting glucose and glucose tolerance.

Real science. Real universities. Not fringe supplement hype.

This was my way out. My alternative to the medication I refused to take.

I ordered a Ceylon cinnamon supplement. Top-rated on Amazon. 1200mg. Took it every day for six weeks.

Fasting glucose: 114. Down from 118.

Four points.

Switched brands. Nature's Bounty, 2000mg plus Chromium. Six more weeks. Didn't miss a single dose.

Fasting glucose: 110.

Better. But still prediabetic. Still in the danger zone.

My follow-up was in seven weeks. If my numbers weren't below the threshold, I knew exactly what was coming. The prescription. The pharmacy. Me on the other side of the counter, filling my own Metformin.

I’m a nurse with Type 2 diabetes. I tried nearly everything. This is what finally made the difference.

My name is Lisa Anderson. I’ve worked as an ICU nurse for 38 years. I’ve held the hands of diabetics in their final moments. I’ve watched metformin steal quality of life from people for decades. I’ve seen where this road can lead.

And I’ve also seen the part almost nobody talks about: metabolic disease silently destroying the kidneys. High blood sugar is not only a blood sugar issue. It is chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, slowly damaging the tiny blood vessels inside your kidneys year after year.

So when my fasting glucose reached 187 and my A1C climbed to 7.2, I already knew what my doctor was going to say before the words left her mouth.

“We need to put you on metformin.”

I smiled. I nodded. I took the prescription.

Then I threw it away three days later.

Not because I was being careless. Not because I was pretending nothing was wrong. But because I had seen what metformin can do to people who take it: nausea, wrecked digestion, constant bathroom trips, brain fog that never seems to lift.

And I had also seen what it does not do.

It does not address the cellular damage that created the diabetes in the first place.

Both paths scared me: uncontrolled diabetes and metformin. Both can still end with declining kidney function. I was looking for a third option.

For three years, I tried everything I could find. Apple cider vinegar before meals. Cinnamon in my coffee. Berberine twice a day. I cut carbs so hard I was eating about 40 grams daily. I walked 10,000 steps. I lifted weights three times a week.

My fasting glucose moved from 187 to 170. My A1C went from 7.2 to 6.8.

Better.

But nowhere near enough.

And the price was brutal. I was drained, irritable, and constantly craving carbs. By 2 PM every day, my brain felt like it was wrapped in cotton. I would wake up at 3 AM to pee, check my glucose out of habit — still around 160 — then lie awake until 4:30 AM, unable to fall back asleep.

I was doing everything “right.”

And still losing.

One night at 11 PM, my husband found me crying in the bathroom, staring at my glucose meter.

After grilled chicken and broccoli.

“Just take the damn metformin,” he said.

“I can’t,” I whispered. “I’ve seen what it does.”

But I was running out of options.

Then something happened that changed everything.

I was discharging a patient — type 2 diabetic, 61 years old, admitted three months earlier with swollen feet and declining kidney function. His creatinine was 1.3. He was moving toward stage 3 kidney disease. The standard pattern for someone whose blood sugar had been uncontrolled for years.

But this time, he looked different.

Lighter. Not just physically. His entire energy was different. His skin had that look people get when inflammation finally starts dropping. He was joking with the physical therapist.

I opened his chart.

His fasting glucose that morning: 94.

Three months earlier at admission: 178.

His creatinine: 1.1.

Down from 1.3.

I walked back into his room.

“Mr. Patterson. Your blood sugar. Your kidneys. What changed?”

He smiled.

“You’re not going to believe me.”

“Try me.”

“I stopped taking metformin.”

My stomach dropped.

“You stopped your medication?”

“Three months ago. Started taking this Ceylon cinnamon supplement my daughter found. Primal Remedies. Took about two weeks and my blood sugar just… dropped. My energy came back. And here’s the thing — my kidney numbers improved. After a month, I felt better than I had in ten years. Talked to my doctor, she ran labs, said whatever I was doing was working. Weaned me off the metformin.”

I just stared at him.

“You’re telling me a cinnamon supplement dropped your fasting glucose by 84 points and improved your kidney function?”

“I’m telling you I sleep through the night now. My brain works again. I’m not chained to a toilet. And my doctor is thrilled with my numbers. Both of them.”

I went home that night and could not sleep.

Not because of my blood sugar.

Because of what he had told me.

I’ve been a nurse for 38 years. I do not believe in magic pills. I do not trust random testimonials. I trust mechanisms and evidence.

So at 2:47 AM, still wide awake, I started researching.

Ceylon cinnamon. True cinnamon — Cinnamomum verum — grown in Sri Lanka. Not the cheap Cassia variety that fills most supplement shelves. The real plant, used medicinally for centuries and now studied in clinical trials for metabolic disease.

The first study I found came from Japan. Type 2 diabetics given clinical-dose Ceylon cinnamon extract showed significant improvements in insulin sensitivity and fasting glucose after 12 weeks.

The second study came from India. Patients with metabolic syndrome showed lower oxidative stress markers and better blood sugar metabolism.

The third came from Italy. Ceylon cinnamon’s main active compound — cinnamaldehyde — reduced inflammatory cytokines and helped protect pancreatic beta cells from oxidative damage.

Then I found the study that made me sit straight up in bed.

It was from Germany, on diabetic nephropathy — kidney damage caused by high blood sugar. Type 2 diabetics with declining kidney function were given a concentrated Ceylon cinnamon extract. After 12 weeks, their proteinuria — the protein leaking through damaged kidneys — dropped by 38%. Their creatinine improved. Their kidney damage was slowing down. In some cases, reversing.

Type 2 diabetes is not just “high blood sugar.” It is chronic inflammation and oxidative stress damaging your cells’ ability to respond to insulin. That same oxidative stress is also attacking the small blood vessels inside your kidneys.

Metformin forces the liver to produce less glucose. It is a chemical override. It can help lower blood sugar, but it does not repair the cellular damage causing insulin resistance in the first place. And it does not reverse kidney damage.

Ceylon cinnamon works differently.

Cinnamaldehyde — its main active compound — activates the same metabolic pathways triggered by exercise. It helps move glucose into cells without depending as heavily on insulin. It shuts down the NLRP3 inflammasome — the master switch behind chronic metabolic inflammation. It lowers the oxidative stress blocking insulin receptors and damaging blood vessels.

It is not forcing the body.

It is removing the interference.

And that matters for the kidneys too. Diabetic kidney damage is not random. It is glucose-driven oxidative stress slowly destroying the tiny blood vessels in your kidneys year after year. Lower the blood sugar. Lower the inflammation. Lower the oxidative stress damaging your glomeruli. Give the kidneys a chance to recover.

"Can I Take Ceylon Cinnamon With Metformin?"

That was the first question I asked when I heard about it. I bet it's the first question you have too.

I was on 1000mg of Metformin twice a day. A1C 8.2. Eight months later? A1C 5.9. Off Metformin completely.

I'm a diabetes nurse. 22 years on the job. Here's what happened.

For 22 years I sat across from patients in the diabetes clinic. I taught them how to use their meters. I explained Metformin. I told them — the way I'd been trained — "your body will adjust. Give it three months."

Three years ago I sat on the other side of that desk.

A1C 7.4. Fasting glucose 162. My doctor wrote the prescription. I picked it up that afternoon.

Metformin. 500mg. Twice a day. The drug I'd explained to other people for two decades.

The first month, my body started telling me things I'd been hearing from patients for years.

The diarrhea hit without warning. Twice a day. Sometimes three.

I'd be teaching a newly diagnosed patient and have to excuse myself. Walk fast down the hallway. Hope I'd make it.

I started mapping every restroom on every floor of the hospital. I memorized which ones had locks that worked. Which ones were empty by 2 PM.

I kept Imodium in my desk. My purse. My car.

By month two, the fatigue settled in.

Not regular tired. The kind that pulls you under at 3 PM and won't let go.

I'd come home from a 9-hour shift and sit in my car for ten minutes. I couldn't make myself walk inside.

I stopped going to my book club. I stopped meeting friends for dinner.

I started saying no to my own grandchildren when they wanted to come over.

By month three, the brain fog had me losing words mid-sentence.

I'd be teaching a class on carb counting. I'd forget what came next. I'd rehearsed it a thousand times.

I started writing notes for things I'd known by heart for fifteen years.

I asked my doctor. He said, "Give it time. Your body will adjust."

It didn't.

At six months my A1C was still 7.6. He bumped me up to 1000mg twice a day.

It got worse.

The diarrhea came back like the first month.

The metallic taste was constant. Coffee, water, even toothpaste tasted like a penny in my mouth.

The fatigue got deeper.

I started reading 1-star reviews on Amazon at 11 PM. Looking for anyone who'd found a way out.

I joined two Facebook groups for Metformin side effects. I read every post. I read every comment. I needed to know I wasn't alone.

At eighteen months my A1C was 8.2.

Higher than when I started. On a higher dose. With worse side effects.

I was at the end of my rope.

I was a 55-year-old diabetes nurse who couldn't leave her own house without planning the route by bathrooms. Who fell asleep in her chair at 7 PM. Who told her patients to "give it time" while privately swallowing Imodium.

And I started wondering. Maybe I was just weak.

Maybe everyone else tolerated this and I was the problem. Maybe I was being dramatic.

That shame is the part nobody talks about.

Every diabetes group online has someone saying "Metformin's not that bad. Just get through the first two weeks."

So you assume you're broken. You assume your body is the problem, not the drug.

You stop telling people what's really happening. Because you're embarrassed.

I sat down with my doctor. I told him everything. Every symptom. Every cancelled plan. Every bathroom map.

I asked him if I could try adding Ceylon cinnamon alongside the medication. With monthly bloodwork to track everything.

In my case, my doctor said yes.

He was clear: don't stop the prescription. Add this in. Track together. Any change to my dose was his call based on the numbers.

That's the only way I'd recommend anyone do this. With your doctor in the loop. Watching the numbers. Making the call.

So I tried Ceylon cinnamon. The first brand was 1200mg, top-rated on Amazon. Six weeks.

My fasting dropped from 162 to 158.

Four points.

I was hopeful for two days. Then I realized I was still in the same place.

I switched to Nature's Bounty. 2000mg with Chromium. Six more weeks.

Fasting glucose: 153.

Better. Still nowhere near where I needed to be. Still on a full dose of Metformin. Still planning my life around bathrooms.

Three months gone.

My follow-up was in seven weeks. If my numbers didn't move, my doctor was going to add a second medication.

I'd seen what that road looks like for my patients. Two drugs. Then three. Then insulin. Then the plastic organizer Sunday through Saturday on the kitchen counter.

I almost gave up.

I almost decided cinnamon just doesn't work. That maybe my diabetes was too far gone.

But after 22 years as a nurse, I know one thing.

When something doesn't work, it's usually not because the science is wrong. It's because the form, the dose, or the delivery is wrong.

So I stopped asking "does cinnamon work?" — the research already answers that.

I started asking "why isn't THIS cinnamon working?"

What I found made me furious.

Most cinnamon supplements are dry powder packed into a capsule. Your body absorbs maybe 15% of the active compounds. The rest passes straight through.

But that's not the worst of it.

The compounds that actually improve insulin sensitivity — the polyphenols — are fat-soluble.

They need a lipid carrier to cross cell membranes and reach your cells.

A dry powder capsule has no fat. Zero. So those compounds float through your gut with nothing to deliver them.

And half the brands on the market use Cassia cinnamon. Not Ceylon.

Cassia contains coumarin. It damages the liver with daily use.

The label just says "cinnamon." They don't have to tell you which kind.

I'd spent three months on supplements that never had a chance of working.

But for the first time in months, I felt something else.

Hope.

Because if the problem was delivery — not the ingredient — then maybe a properly formulated version existed.

I dug through forums. Reviews. Recommendations from women whose numbers had actually moved.

One name kept appearing: Primal Remedies.

True Ceylon cinnamon from Sri Lanka. 7,200mg per serving. Every softgel infused with organic MCT oil — the lipid carrier that shuttles polyphenols across cell membranes. Third-party tested. Safe alongside other medications.

I ordered it. My follow-up was five weeks away.

I took my first dose on a Wednesday. Three softgels with breakfast.

Expected nothing.

That afternoon, the 3 PM crash didn't come. I worked until 5:30 still feeling sharp.

Probably a fluke.

Next morning, fasting glucose: 144. Down from 153.

One week: 138. Then 131. Then 125.

Two weeks: consistently in the 120s. Post-meal spikes flattening.

Where lunch used to push me to 215, I was seeing 165.

Three weeks: 115. The afternoon crash was gone. The diarrhea I'd lived with for over a year started easing.

Four weeks: 108.

I went to my follow-up. A1C: 6.4.

My doctor pulled up the chart. Looked at the history. Looked at me.

"What changed?"

I told him.

He nodded. "These numbers are excellent. Let's start tapering. Cut the morning dose in half this month."

Thirty days later: A1C 6.1. Fasting 99. Evening dose cut.

Sixty days after that: A1C 5.9. Fasting 92.

He looked at me and said, "I don't see a reason to keep you on Metformin anymore."

Four months later, I haven't filled a prescription.

The diarrhea is gone. The metallic taste is gone. The brain fog is gone. The afternoon crash is gone.

I see my grandkids without a strategy. I drive to the lake without a bathroom map.

If you've tried cinnamon and it didn't work, it probably wasn't you.

It wasn't that your body was broken. It wasn't that your diabetes was too far gone.

It was probably dry powder with no absorption system. Cassia instead of Ceylon. A fraction of the dose your cells actually needed.

And every month on the wrong product is another month of side effects. Another month closer to the next prescription.

If you're on Metformin and you're tired of side effects with no real progress — talk to your doctor about adding properly formulated Ceylon cinnamon.

In my case, my doctor approved it alongside my medication. The numbers spoke for themselves.

True Ceylon. 7,200mg. MCT oil delivery.

You might be surprised what happens when your cells get the real thing.

ads.primaryText:
"Can I Take Ceylon Cinnamon With Metformin?"

That was the first question I asked when I heard about it. I bet it's the first question you have too.

I was on 1000mg of Metformin twice a day. A1C 8.2. Eight months later? A1C 5.9. Off Metformin completely.

I'm a diabetes nurse. 22 years on the job. Here's what happened.

For 22 years I sat across from patients in the diabetes clinic. I taught them how to use their meters. I explained Metformin. I told them — the way I'd been trained — "your body will adjust. Give it three months."

Three years ago I sat on the other side of that desk.

A1C 7.4. Fasting glucose 162. My doctor wrote the prescription. I picked it up that afternoon.

Metformin. 500mg. Twice a day. The drug I'd explained to other people for two decades.

The first month, my body started telling me things I'd been hearing from patients for years.

The diarrhea hit without warning. Twice a day. Sometimes three.

I'd be teaching a newly diagnosed patient and have to excuse myself. Walk fast down the hallway. Hope I'd make it.

I started mapping every restroom on every floor of the hospital. I memorized which ones had locks that worked. Which ones were empty by 2 PM.

I kept Imodium in my desk. My purse. My car.

By month two, the fatigue settled in.

Not regular tired. The kind that pulls you under at 3 PM and won't let go.

I'd come home from a 9-hour shift and sit in my car for ten minutes. I couldn't make myself walk inside.

I stopped going to my book club. I stopped meeting friends for dinner.

I started saying no to my own grandchildren when they wanted to come over.

By month three, the brain fog had me losing words mid-sentence.

I'd be teaching a class on carb counting. I'd forget what came next. I'd rehearsed it a thousand times.

I started writing notes for things I'd known by heart for fifteen years.

I asked my doctor. He said, "Give it time. Your body will adjust."

It didn't.

At six months my A1C was still 7.6. He bumped me up to 1000mg twice a day.

It got worse.

The diarrhea came back like the first month.

The metallic taste was constant. Coffee, water, even toothpaste tasted like a penny in my mouth.

The fatigue got deeper.

I started reading 1-star reviews on Amazon at 11 PM. Looking for anyone who'd found a way out.

I joined two Facebook groups for Metformin side effects. I read every post. I read every comment. I needed to know I wasn't alone.

At eighteen months my A1C was 8.2.

Higher than when I started. On a higher dose. With worse side effects.

I was at the end of my rope.

I was a 55-year-old diabetes nurse who couldn't leave her own house without planning the route by bathrooms. Who fell asleep in her chair at 7 PM. Who told her patients to "give it time" while privately swallowing Imodium.

And I started wondering. Maybe I was just weak.

Maybe everyone else tolerated this and I was the problem. Maybe I was being dramatic.

That shame is the part nobody talks about.

Every diabetes group online has someone saying "Metformin's not that bad. Just get through the first two weeks."

So you assume you're broken. You assume your body is the problem, not the drug.

You stop telling people what's really happening. Because you're embarrassed.

I sat down with my doctor. I told him everything. Every symptom. Every cancelled plan. Every bathroom map.

I asked him if I could try adding Ceylon cinnamon alongside the medication. With monthly bloodwork to track everything.

In my case, my doctor said yes.

He was clear: don't stop the prescription. Add this in. Track together. Any change to my dose was his call based on the numbers.

That's the only way I'd recommend anyone do this. With your doctor in the loop. Watching the numbers. Making the call.

So I tried Ceylon cinnamon. The first brand was 1200mg, top-rated on Amazon. Six weeks.

My fasting dropped from 162 to 158.

Four points.

I was hopeful for two days. Then I realized I was still in the same place.

I switched to Nature's Bounty. 2000mg with Chromium. Six more weeks.

Fasting glucose: 153.

Better. Still nowhere near where I needed to be. Still on a full dose of Metformin. Still planning my life around bathrooms.

Three months gone.

My follow-up was in seven weeks. If my numbers didn't move, my doctor was going to add a second medication.

I'd seen what that road looks like for my patients. Two drugs. Then three. Then insulin. Then the plastic organizer Sunday through Saturday on the kitchen counter.

I almost gave up.

I almost decided cinnamon just doesn't work. That maybe my diabetes was too far gone.

But after 22 years as a nurse, I know one thing.

When something doesn't work, it's usually not because the science is wrong. It's because the form, the dose, or the delivery is wrong.

So I stopped asking "does cinnamon work?" — the research already answers that.

I started asking "why isn't THIS cinnamon working?"

What I found made me furious.

Most cinnamon supplements are dry powder packed into a capsule. Your body absorbs maybe 15% of the active compounds. The rest passes straight through.

But that's not the worst of it.

The compounds that actually improve insulin sensitivity — the polyphenols — are fat-soluble.

They need a lipid carrier to cross cell membranes and reach your cells.

A dry powder capsule has no fat. Zero. So those compounds float through your gut with nothing to deliver them.

And half the brands on the market use Cassia cinnamon. Not Ceylon.

Cassia contains coumarin. It damages the liver with daily use.

The label just says "cinnamon." They don't have to tell you which kind.

I'd spent three months on supplements that never had a chance of working.

But for the first time in months, I felt something else.

Hope.

Because if the problem was delivery — not the ingredient — then maybe a properly formulated version existed.

I dug through forums. Reviews. Recommendations from women whose numbers had actually moved.

One name kept appearing: Primal Remedies.

True Ceylon cinnamon from Sri Lanka. 7,200mg per serving. Every softgel infused with organic MCT oil — the lipid carrier that shuttles polyphenols across cell membranes. Third-party tested. Safe alongside other medications.

I ordered it. My follow-up was five weeks away.

I took my first dose on a Wednesday. Three softgels with breakfast.

Expected nothing.

That afternoon, the 3 PM crash didn't come. I worked until 5:30 still feeling sharp.

Probably a fluke.

Next morning, fasting glucose: 144. Down from 153.

One week: 138. Then 131. Then 125.

Two weeks: consistently in the 120s. Post-meal spikes flattening.

Where lunch used to push me to 215, I was seeing 165.

Three weeks: 115. The afternoon crash was gone. The diarrhea I'd lived with for over a year started easing.

Four weeks: 108.

I went to my follow-up. A1C: 6.4.

My doctor pulled up the chart. Looked at the history. Looked at me.

"What changed?"

I told him.

He nodded. "These numbers are excellent. Let's start tapering. Cut the morning dose in half this month."

Thirty days later: A1C 6.1. Fasting 99. Evening dose cut.

Sixty days after that: A1C 5.9. Fasting 92.

He looked at me and said, "I don't see a reason to keep you on Metformin anymore."

Four months later, I haven't filled a prescription.

The diarrhea is gone. The metallic taste is gone. The brain fog is gone. The afternoon crash is gone.

I see my grandkids without a strategy. I drive to the lake without a bathroom map.

If you've tried cinnamon and it didn't work, it probably wasn't you.

It wasn't that your body was broken. It wasn't that your diabetes was too far gone.

It was probably dry powder with no absorption system. Cassia instead of Ceylon. A fraction of the dose your cells actually needed.

And every month on the wrong product is another month of side effects. Another month closer to the next prescription.

If you're on Metformin and you're tired of side effects with no real progress — talk to your doctor about adding properly formulated Ceylon cinnamon.

In my case, my doctor approved it alongside my medication. The numbers spoke for themselves.

Primal Remedies is the only brand I've found that gets all three right.

True Ceylon. 7,200mg. MCT oil delivery.

You might be surprised what happens when your cells get the real thing.

👉 https://primal-remedies.com/pages/lp1-c-met

— Karen Whitfield, RN, CDE
